parts.text:
1
What is a reasonable estimate of the cross-sectional area of the wire in a paper clip?
A
1 × 10–3
m2
B
8 × 10–5
m2
C
8 × 10–7
m2
D
1 × 10–9
m2

hints: Visualise the thickness of paper-clip wire - its diameter is roughly $1 \text{ mm}$, so its radius is about $0.5 \text{ mm} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$.
Recall the circular cross-section rule $A = \pi r^2$ for the wire, so squaring a radius of order $10^{-4} \text{ m}$ must give an area of order $10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$.
Test each power of ten by working backwards to diameter - $10^{-3} \text{ m}^2$ means cm size and $10^{-9} \text{ m}^2$ means micrometre size, neither of which fits a paper clip.
walkthrough: Estimate the wire diameter from everyday experience: paper-clip wire is about $1 \text{ mm} = 1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ thick, so radius $r \approx 0.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$.
State the physical rule for a circular cross-section: $A = \pi r^2$, with $A$ in $\text{m}^2$ when $r$ is in $\text{m}$.
Substitute the estimate: $A \approx \pi \times (5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m})^2 = \pi \times 25 \times 10^{-8} \text{ m}^2 \approx 7.9 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$.
Compare orders of magnitude: $10^{-3} \text{ m}^2$ and $10^{-5} \text{ m}^2$ are $10^4$ and $10^2$ times too large, and $10^{-9} \text{ m}^2$ is $10^2$ times too small.
The value near $8 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$ matches the estimate. This is option C.

A.explanation: An area of $1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^2$ implies a diameter of several cm, which is the size of a pipe not paper-clip wire.

B.explanation: An area of $8 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^2$ implies a diameter of about $1 \text{ cm}$, far thicker than real paper-clip wire.

C.explanation: A radius of about $5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$ gives $A = \pi r^2 \approx 8 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$, matching paper-clip wire.

D.explanation: An area of $1 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}^2$ implies a diameter of only tens of micrometres, thinner than a human hair.
